account: In a Globe and Mail report of 26 December 2023, Joe Castaldo described how Wes Ramage of Calgary, who is blind, uses Envision Glasses. They are a Google Glass headset with Envision's AI software. The Globe and Mail reports that Ramage first came across Envision in 2022 and that he serves as an unpaid beta tester for the company. He uses the glasses to describe scenes, identify clothing colors, find empty chairs and misplaced objects, read street signs when navigating transit and read menus. The article does not date the individual uses. Ramage said that the glasses bring a level of comfort he had not had in many years. He described heading out each morning with his glasses, keys and wallet. The article gives a price of US$1,899 to US$3,499 and reports that a provincial program covered part of his cost. It also profiles Nayla Farah of Toronto using the Be My AI app, covered by an existing record. Envision's product page says that the glasses are built on Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2. They offer Instant Text, Scan Text, Describe Scene and an Ask Envision feature on an OpenAI model. In a crossover study published on 8 January 2025, researchers at Lighthouse Guild and Amsterdam UMC found that Envision Glasses raised the odds that 25 people with vision loss could complete all six text tasks and that they read a street sign faster than without a device. Ramage was not part of that study.

ai_role.statement: The glasses' text recognition and scene description produced the readings Ramage relies on. The Globe article is the only outcome source. It attributes the comfort to the glasses in the user's own words. No clinical or task measurement exists in the sources.

fields.headline: *Envision Glasses* read signs and menus for a blind man in Calgary
fields.title: Envision Glasses read street signs, menus and scenes for Wes Ramage in Calgary, bringing comfort he had not had in years

fields.account: In a Globe and Mail report of 26 December 2023, Joe Castaldo described how Wes Ramage of Calgary, who is blind, uses Envision Glasses. They are a Google Glass headset with Envision's AI software. The Globe and Mail reports that Ramage first came across Envision in 2022 and that he serves as an unpaid beta tester for the company. He uses the glasses to describe scenes, identify clothing colors, find empty chairs and misplaced objects, read street signs when navigating transit and read menus. The article does not date the individual uses. Ramage said that the glasses bring a level of comfort he had not had in many years. He described heading out each morning with his glasses, keys and wallet. The article gives a price of US$1,899 to US$3,499 and reports that a provincial program covered part of his cost. It also profiles Nayla Farah of Toronto using the Be My AI app, covered by an existing record. Envision's product page says that the glasses are built on Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2. They offer Instant Text, Scan Text, Describe Scene and an Ask Envision feature on an OpenAI model. In a crossover study published on 8 January 2025, researchers at Lighthouse Guild and Amsterdam UMC found that Envision Glasses raised the odds that 25 people with vision loss could complete all six text tasks and that they read a street sign faster than without a device. Ramage was not part of that study.
